ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

famous.name: Charles Lewis Tiffany
famous.story_individual:
Charles Lewis Tiffany was an American businessman who founded the iconic luxury jewelry company Tiffany & Co. in 1837. Starting with a $1,000 loan from his father, he and partner John B. Young opened a small stationery and gift shop in New York City that eventually grew into one of the world's premier jewelry retailers.

Tiffany revolutionized retail through several innovations, including creating America's first retail catalog (the "Blue Book") in 1845 and introducing the English sterling silver standard to the United States in 1851. He is also credited with creating the famous "Tiffany Setting" six-prong engagement ring in 1886 and establishing the signature "Tiffany Blue Box" as a symbol of luxury.

A savvy businessman, Tiffany built his company's reputation by selling only the finest goods and making strategic investments, such as purchasing European diamonds during political unrest in 1848. His company expanded internationally with branches in Paris and London, and gained prestige by acquiring and selling French Crown Jewels in 1887.

During the Civil War, Tiffany shifted much of his business to manufacturing swords, medals, and other war materials, showing his adaptability as an entrepreneur. His most enduring legacy was transforming Tiffany & Co. into North America's premier jewelry company, valued at over $2 million at the time of his death.

Information on his mtDNA haplogroup was sourced from WikiTree.

famous.name: Kaspar Hauser
famous.story_individual:
Kaspar Hauser mysteriously appeared in Nuremberg on May 26, 1828, estimated to be around 16 years old, barely able to walk or speak, and carrying a letter addressed to a cavalry captain. He claimed to have spent his entire life confined to a dark cell, fed only bread and water by an unseen caretaker - a story that gained credibility as he showed remarkable progress in learning to communicate while maintaining unusual behaviors consistent with extreme isolation. Two opposing theories emerged regarding his origins: either he was an abducted prince of the Grand Duchy of Baden, or he was a liar and fraud who deceived the honorable but naive citizens of Nuremberg and Ansbach.

Rumors supporting the first theory circulated around 1829, suggesting Hauser was the hereditary prince of Baden who had been switched at birth with a commoner - a theory that persisted for nearly two centuries. However, a 2024 study definitively ruled out this possibility by testing hair shafts attributed to Kaspar and confirming they matched previously tested bloodstains from his trousers and underwear. The analysis demonstrated that Hauser's maternal haplogroup was W, which differed from the House of Baden's H1b haplogroup. This genetic evidence conclusively disproved the royal connection, though the debate about whether he was genuinely isolated or an impostor continues.

Hauser's life ended tragically on December 14, 1833, when he stumbled home in Ansbach with a deep chest wound, claiming a stranger had stabbed him in the court garden. Forensic examiners at the time agreed the wound might have been self-inflicted, with many scholars theorizing he had wounded himself to revive public interest but fatally injured himself by mistake. He died three days later on December 17, leaving behind one of Europe's most enduring historical mysteries.

Reference

  • Walther Parson, Christina Amory, Turi King, Michaela Preick, Cordula Berger, Anna König, Gabriela Huber, Katja Anslinger, Birgit Bayer, Gottfried Weichhold, Timo Sänger, Sabine Lutz-Bonengel, Heidi Pfeiffer, Michael Hofreiter, Dietmar Pfründer, Carsten Hohoff, Bernd Brinkmann, Kaspar Hauser’s alleged noble origin – New molecular genetic analyses resolve the controversy, iScience, Volume 27, Issue 9, 2024, 110539, ISSN 2589-0042, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2024.110539.

famous.name: Martha Stewart
famous.story_individual:
Martha Helen Stewart has revolutionized the American lifestyle industry for interior design and homemaking. She is also the first female self-made billionaire in the United States.

Her journey to becoming a household name began in 1982 with the publication of Entertaining by Martha Stewart. This success led to the creation of Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia, the first multi-channel lifestyle company, which grew to encompass publishing, broadcasting, merchandising, and e-commerce. As an Emmy Award-winning television host and author of 99 lifestyle books, she built a successful merchandising business offering home products through various retail and online outlets.

In 2004, Stewart faced legal challenges and served five months in federal prison for charges related to insider trading. Following her release in 2005, she engineered a remarkable comeback, returning to Martha Stewart Living and rebuilding her empire. Her influence on American home life continues to expand through her media platforms and product lines, where she shares her expertise on cooking, entertaining, gardening, and decorating with millions of devoted followers.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was revealed in episode 8 of the first season of Finding Your Roots, which aired in 2012.

famous.name: Mika Häkkinen
famous.story_individual:
Mika Häkkinen, known as “The Flying Finn,” is a Finnish former professional racing driver who is widely recognized for his successful career in Formula One. Born in Vantaa, Finland, Häkkinen's interest in racing was evident from an early age. He started his racing career in karting and steadily climbed through the ranks to reach Formula One.

Häkkinen's Formula One career began with the Lotus team in 1991. After two seasons, he moved to McLaren in 1993, where he stayed for the rest of his career. In 1998 and 1999, Häkkinen achieved the pinnacle of motorsport success, winning back-to-back World Championships. His smooth and precise driving style, combined with his calm and focused demeanor, earned him the nickname "the Flying Finn." He is one of only three Finnish Formula One drivers to win the World Championship and the only driver from Finland to win the World Championship more than once.

In 2001, Häkkinen announced a sabbatical from Formula One that eventually became a permanent retirement. He later returned to racing in the Deutsche Tourenwagen Masters (DTM), a popular touring car championship, where he drove for Mercedes-Benz from 2005 to 2007.

After retiring from competitive racing, Häkkinen has remained involved in motorsport, working as a brand ambassador and driver mentor. He is often hailed as one of the greatest drivers in the history of Formula One for his remarkable talent and sportsmanship.

Mika tested his DNA with FamilyTreeDNA for a Finnish program, and the results were presented in 2021 with the title The DNA of the World Champion. His maternal line was found to belong to mtDNA haplogroup W1.

May 2023 correction: An earlier version incorrectly had Mika associated with a different Y-DNA haplogroup.

famous.name: Anna Peck Sill
famous.story_individual:
Anna Peck Sill was a pioneering American educator who dedicated her life to advancing women's education in the 19th century.

In 1847, Sill founded the Rockford Female Seminary in Illinois, which would later become Rockford University. As its first principal, she challenged the prevailing attitudes of her time by implementing a rigorous academic curriculum that included subjects typically reserved for men, such as mathematics, science, and ancient languages. Her educational philosophy was influenced by Mary Lyon's approach at Mount Holyoke, and she worked to create similarly high standards at Rockford.

Under Sill's leadership, the institution grew from a small seminary into a respected women's college. By the time she retired in 1884, five thousand women had graduated under her guidance. Her impact on women's education in the Midwest was profound, demonstrating that women were fully capable of pursuing advanced studies. Throughout her tenure, she maintained high academic standards while fostering an environment that encouraged intellectual growth. Her legacy lives on in Rockford University, which continues to operate as a coeducational institution today.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was determined by mtFull testing of her matrilineal relative and documented on WikiTree.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.
